newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't resorts to maneuver to save reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't resorts to maneuver to save reform.

text.p: The Brazilian government resorted to a controversial maneuver in the Chamber of Deputies late Tuesday because it feared it was heading for defeat over a key amendment to its civil service reform bill, analysts said.
The episode also cast doubt on the government's ability to push through the rest of its reform program as next year's presidential elections start to distract Congress, they said.

"It sounds absurd, but the government can't count on getting the 308 votes it needs (to approve constitutional amendments) from the 410 deputies who in theory are its allies," said Ricardo Pedreira, an analyst with consultants Santa Fe Ideias.

Government whips infuriated left-wing opposition parties Tuesday when they forwarded a motion challenging the legitimacy of four amendments to the civil service reform bill and proposing they be sent to a lower house committee.

The motion was approved easily, would effectively bury the amendments, one of which would have maintained the jobs-for-life guarantees of public sector workers, because the government needs only a simple majority in the panel to kill them.
On the floor of the lower house it would have required a three-fifths majority or 308 votes.
"The government did the manoeuver because it was certain it did not have the 308 votes to avoid the reform being disfigured," Pedreira said.

Already tense relations between the government and the Chamber of Deputies soured recently when President Fernando Henrique Cardoso withdrew his support for a proposal which would have exempted lawmakers from a pay cap included in the civil service reform bill.
Political analyst Paulo Kramer said lawmakers were also worried about supporting reforms which the government has failed to sell to public opinion.

"Unfortunately, the image of the civil service reform bill is that it will put thousands of public sector workers on the dole while people think the pension reform will steal money from the wallets of poor pensioners," Kramer said.
Newspapers have reported recently that presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral would be replaced later in the year as part of a new public relations drive by the government.

In the short-term, however, it must press ahead with voting on several remaining amendments to the civil service reform bill and then approve the bill in a second round of voting on the floor of the lower house.
Left-wing parties, which likened Tuesday's manoeuver to a military coup, have said they might block those votes.

The government also has to make progress on its pension reform bill which lost most of its most important points during voting in the Chamber of Deputies last year and is currently being rewritten in the Senate.
The new-look text faces a committee-level vote in the upper house, two votes on the floor of the Senate and, if approved, will then return to the lower house for approval of the changes.
A bill allowing Cardoso to run for re-election next year has also run into trouble in the Senate.

Many senators plan to run as state governors in 1998 and want to rewrite the bill to prevent sitting governors from remaining in office during their re-election campaigns. Any such change to the bill would require another round of voting in the Chamber of Deputies, something the government wants to avoid.

Analyst Pedreira said that while the reforms might yet be approved by the end of the year, when Congress will succumb to election fever, the government would probably end up calling a special "revisionary session" of Congress in 1999 to deepen them.

In a revisionary session, constitutional amendments can be approved with only a simple majority. To call such a session, however, the government would have to approve a constitutional amendment during the current session of Congress, requiring the normal three-fifths majority.
"They're keeping quiet about it for fear of making the deputies even more rebellious but it's a strong possibility," Pedreira said.
(( -- Brasilia newsroom 5561 2230358))
